title: Event Handling
subtitle: onClick, onChange, synthetic events, preventing defaults, and bubbling
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: UIs need to respond to user actions — clicks, keyboard input, form submissions, hover. Plain DOM event listeners (addEventListener) are managed outside React's lifecycle, leading to stale references and memory leaks.
whyItExists.solution: React uses a synthetic event system: you attach handlers as props (onClick, onChange) and React handles delegation — one listener at the root, dispatching to the right handler. Synthetic events normalize cross-browser differences and clean up automatically.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any user interaction: button clicks, form input changes, form submission, keyboard shortcuts, drag events.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Global events (window resize, document keydown) need useEffect + addEventListener because React's synthetic events only cover DOM elements rendered by React.

explainModes.beginner: To respond to a click, add onClick to a button: <button onClick={handleClick}>. The handler is a JavaScript function. For text inputs, onChange fires on every keystroke: <input onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)}>. The e object gives you information about the event.
explainModes.simple: onClick, onChange, onSubmit, onKeyDown, onFocus, onBlur — all camelCase. Handler receives a synthetic event object: e.target (the element), e.target.value (input value), e.preventDefault() (stop form submit/link navigation), e.stopPropagation() (stop event bubbling). Don't call the function: onClick={handleClick} not onClick={handleClick()}.
explainModes.standard: Synthetic events are pooled in older React (reused for performance) — don't access them asynchronously in pre-React 17. React 17+ switched to native events, but the interface is the same. Event delegation: React attaches a single listener to the root container, not to each element. This is efficient and avoids listener leaks. Pass data to handlers: <button onClick={() => handleDelete(item.id)}>.
explainModes.technical: React's synthetic event wraps the native event but has the same interface (target, currentTarget, preventDefault, stopPropagation, nativeEvent). Bubbling: events bubble through the React tree (not the DOM tree, which matters for portals). Capture phase: use onClickCapture for capture-phase handling. useCallback stabilizes event handlers so React.memo children don't unnecessarily re-render when parent re-renders.
explainModes.deepDive: Event pooling history: React 16 and earlier reused SyntheticEvent objects (pooled) — accessing event.target asynchronously gave null. e.persist() was needed. React 17+ removed pooling — events are not reused. The switch also moved event delegation from document to the React root, enabling multiple React roots on the same page without cross-root event conflicts. Portals and event bubbling: a portal's events bubble through the React component tree, not the DOM tree — a click inside a portal modal will trigger onClick handlers on its React ancestors even though the DOM ancestors are different.

questions.question: What is the difference between `onClick={handleClick}` and `onClick={handleClick()}`?
options: There is no difference — both work the same way
onClick={handleClick} passes the function to be called on click; onClick={handleClick()} calls the function immediately during render and passes its return value
onClick={handleClick()} is the correct syntax for event handlers
onClick={handleClick} only works for button elements
questions.explanation: onClick={handleClick} gives React a reference to the function — React will call it when the button is clicked. onClick={handleClick()} calls handleClick immediately when the component renders (before any click), and passes the return value (probably undefined) as the event handler. This is a very common React mistake. Always pass the function reference, not its result.

faq.q: How do I access the input value in an onChange handler?
faq.a: Use e.target.value: <input onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)} />. For checkboxes, it's e.target.checked. For select elements, it's also e.target.value (the value of the selected option). In TypeScript: (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => e.target.value.

usedIn: every interactive form and button in React apps
examples: <div onClick={() => selectItem(id)} onKeyDown={e => e.key === 'Enter' && selectItem(id)} tabIndex={0}>
